rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded early triplet separates with a shallower slope. This diagnostic also measures the time cost and the response of the moderately resolved later pair.

Test a substantial temperature increase at the original gradient slope to shift selectivity within the early triplet. Higher temperature should also shorten retention, potentially improving resolution without a time penalty.

At 60 C only one pair remains below target, and the last peak has nearly two minutes of time margin. Test a shallower gradient to determine whether that pair improves enough to reach full resolution near the 10-minute limit.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper gradient instead. This should improve that pair and shorten the run, while checking that the neighboring pair retains adequate resolution.

Slope changes alone have not fully resolved the high-temperature triplet. Test the opposite temperature limit to look for a more favorable elution order and stronger selectivity before refining the gradient window.

Return to the favorable high temperature and shift the starting organic fraction to change selectivity within the critical triplet. This tests a new control variable while retaining ample elution strength and a short expected last-peak time.
Injection 7 achieved the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark and test a two-minute shorter gradient. This seeks a faster fully resolved method while checking the two closest pairs.
Shorten the gradient by another grid step to locate the full-resolution speed limit. Injection 8 remains a maximum-score fallback if either close pair drops below R = 1.5.

Slightly narrow the gradient window to recover resolution in both marginal pairs while keeping the eight-minute gradient. The last peak previously eluted near 0.64 organic, so 0.85 should still provide ample elution strength.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves the critical triplet enough to permit faster elution. Compare against injections 9 and 10, watching both triplet selectivity and compression of the earliest peaks.

Test a five-degree temperature reduction at the nearly fully resolved eight-minute method. A modest selectivity shift may lift both marginal triplet gaps above 1.5 without requiring a shallower gradient.

Keep the favorable starting composition and temperature while trimming the endpoint and gradient duration. This slope lies between the resolved injection 10 and marginal injection 9, testing a faster full-resolution boundary with the endpoint still above the last peak’s estimated elution composition.

Injection 13’s rounded CRF masks a pair just below full resolution, so use the actual resolution values as the criterion. Slightly reduce the slope from injection 10 to establish a larger resolution margin while retaining a last-peak time comfortably below 10 minutes.

At phi0 = 0.20 the second triplet gap improved, but the first became limiting. Test a shallower gradient to recover that first gap and assess whether this starting composition offers a more robust fully resolved method.

Back off one endpoint step from injection 13 to bring its marginal pair above R = 1.5 while retaining the six-minute gradient. The last peak should elute near the gradient endpoint; verify that any final hold does not materially extend retention.

Compare with injection 10 at the same gradient slope but a lower starting organic fraction to isolate the effect of the gradient window on triplet selectivity. This checks the remaining nearby starting-composition option while preserving the established maximum-score methods.

Back off one duration step from injection 15’s marginal resolution at phi0 = 0.20. This should test whether that starting composition can achieve full resolution with balanced triplet gaps and no time penalty.

The fastest confirmed fully resolved method remains injection 10. With maximum CRF already secured, test whether a shallower gradient at the best starting composition provides greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test the remaining endpoint step between injections 9 and 10 to refine the fastest full-resolution boundary. The critical pair will likely be very close to R = 1.5, so judge success by its resolution rather than the rounded CRF.

Injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; its next steeper endpoint step failed. Test an intermediate slope between injections 8 and 7 to obtain more resolution margin than the fastest method while eluting sooner than injection 7.

Refine the tradeoff between speed and resolution margin using a slope between injections 14 and 21. This should retain maximum CRF with a larger critical-pair margin than the fastest confirmed method, while keeping the last peak below seven minutes.

Test a trimmed endpoint with the same initial gradient slope as injection 22, which fully resolved the early critical pairs. Refine between injections 8 and 21 to seek a modest resolution margin with less retention time than injection 21. Injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, and the campaign has already achieved the maximum possible CRF.
